newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy opens welfare can of worms as talks begin.
newsitem.headline: Italy opens welfare can of worms as talks begin.

text.p: The Italian government on Wednesday began long-awaited and potentially explosive talks with union leaders and employers on how to reform the costly welfare state.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi, just back from a marathon session to draft the new European Union treaty in Amsterdam, opened what is expected to be a long, hot summer of negotiation.

Labour Minister Tiziano Treu said the first meeting, between the centre-left government and 31 groups including employers' body Confindustria, the three main union confederations and trade bodies, would be largely given over to setting the agenda.
"We'll have a preliminary overview, work out a timetable and discuss working methods. There will be plenty to do," he said.

Italy is under pressure to carry out a convincing reform of social spending -- and to shake up its pensions system -- to prove that public finances will be kept under control before the planned 1999 launch of the single European currency.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi was upbeat about the outcome. "The negotiations are opening amid confidence about a positive outcome," he told financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
Prodi has already pushed through close to 100 trillion lire ($59 billion) of cuts and savings since he took office in May 1996 in a race to qualify Italy for membership from the start.

But he has delayed the thorny question of streamlining the welfare state, which is likely to pit his centre-left coalition against powerful unions and a key ally, the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which will countenance no cuts.
Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti, whose party secures Prodi's majority in parliament, warned the government that its support was not guaranteed.
"We would have preferred the reform to be preceded by the definition of a common position of the (ruling) majority on such a decisive issue for the country," Bertinotti said.

"That didn't happen. The government chose otherwise and so the whole majority doesn't have to be committed by its positions," he said. "In any case, Refoundation will push for a good reform of the welfare state with a new policy for jobs and no cuts in social spending or pensions."
Ministers have already said they expect to have to give up their holidays in order to hammer out a deal by September, when the 1998 budget must be drafted and presented to parliament.
The government has already announced that the budget will contain about 25 trillion lire of deficit-cutting measures, but has not yet gone into detail of where the savings will be made.

In a three-year document of financial targets last month, it said Italy needed to carry out reforms to its system of welfare provision and called for a shake-up of pensions, but steered clear of how this would be achieved.
Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio has said that about 10 trillion lire of the planned 25 trillion lire of measures in next year's budget should come from welfare state savings.
He has also recommended that pension spending, forecast to grow by six percent next year, should be more in line with the expected two percent growth in Gross Domestic Product.
Confindustria said earlier this month that it wanted the negotiations to include a review of Italy's last stab at reforming pensions -- a partial reform carried out in 1995.
Unions had said they wanted no changes to that deal, which introduced a graduated increase in the pensionable age and the opening up of a pay-as-you-go contributions system.

Confindustria chairman Giorgio Fossa has said he wants the length of service pensions, which allow many Italians to draw a pension years before reaching pensionable age, to be abolished. ($1=1,690 lire)
